title: AUSA 2026: Hegseth Pushes Autonomy Command and a 33-Nation Drone Marketplace as Counter-Drone Fast-Tracking Goes Live
subhead: The US Army's annual convention became a launchpad for autonomous warfare reform — a new drone-buying marketplace now open to 33 countries, a Pentagon memo cutting counter-drone approvals from months to days, and Hegseth's push for a four-star Autonomous Warfare Command.

sections.heading: AUSA 2026: Hegseth Bets on Autonomy — and a New Four-Star Command
sections.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used the Association of the US Army (AUSA) annual conference in Washington on Oct. 14 to push a broad restructuring around autonomous and robotic weapons. Speaking on an autonomy panel, Hegseth framed the effort around speed of acquisition: the people who buy platforms 'need to be right there, up with the warfighter... who understand how to iterate it and change on and innovate on it,' according to Breaking Defense.

The centerpiece is Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM), a recently announced four-star command intended to hold service-like authorities to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force. Congress must still sign off. In the meantime, the Pentagon has moved its Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for autonomy under a new umbrella initiative, Project Agincourt, and is folding the Defense Autonomous Working Group (DAWG) into a new Task Force Autonomous Warfare inside SOCOM. Breaking Defense reports the Pentagon has laid out plans to spend nearly $55 billion on DAWG, though it remains unclear how much Congress will actually approve given the stalled fiscal 2027 spending bill and a separate reconciliation request.

The show floor reinforced the theme: Ukrainian firms including Stellarion (fiber-optic drones) and Tencore exhibited alongside US primes, while RTX showed its DeepFires autonomous launcher and GM Defense displayed an autonomous ISV-Utility configured for counter-drone and electronic-warfare payloads.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is trying to convert industrial-base rhetoric into an acquisition structure that can actually field autonomous systems at speed. AUTOWARCOM and Project Agincourt are the mechanism — but both remain dependent on a defense budget Congress has not passed.

sections.heading: Army Opens Its Drone Marketplace to 33 Nations — With $7B in Counter-UAS Vehicles Already Awarded
sections.body:
Eight more countries — Canada, Croatia, Egypt, Japan, Kuwait, Morocco, Albania and Panama — signed a statement of intent on Oct. 13 to join the US Army's Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Marketplace, bringing total participation to 33 nations, according to Defense News. The marketplace launched in March 2026 with nine European signers.

Assistant Secretary of the Army for acquisition Brent Ingraham said the platform has processed $800 million in transactions and that the Army has awarded counter-UAS contract vehicles worth $7 billion through it. It operates as a government-to-government 'fast lane' for foreign military sales of equipment pre-vetted for cybersecurity and exportability; a parallel C-UAS Marketplace is run by Joint Interagency Task Force 401.

Ingraham's rationale was blunt: cheap drones have forced militaries to answer with expensive missiles — a reference to reports that the US used virtually all of its long-range precision missiles during the Iran war. 'There is no silver bullet. None of us can do it alone,' he said, describing a layered approach spanning sensors, command and control, electronic warfare, interceptors and directed energy.
sections.whyItMatters: This turns a US domestic procurement tool into an allied export channel — effectively a pre-cleared foreign military sales conveyor belt. It could compress the cycle from requirement to delivery for partners who previously waited years for US drones and interceptors.

sections.heading: Pentagon Orders Counter-Drone Approvals Cut From Months to Days
sections.body:
The Department of Defense issued a memorandum directing officials to accelerate approvals for counter-drone systems and strip out bureaucratic hurdles, The Defense Post reported on Oct. 14. Under the directive, senior officials must set an expedited approval timeline for validated counter-UAS systems — cutting a process that 'typically takes months' down to weeks or days. Reviews of pending weapons and defense systems must also be expedited, with a 10-day review period beginning once required documentation is received.

The move lands the same week as AUSA, where counter-drone hardware dominated the show floor: BAE Systems displayed layered directed-energy and kinetic counter-UAS systems, Leonardo DRS launched its new cxMHR 360-degree radar with a detection range exceeding 205 miles, and L3Harris confirmed the Army had received its first VAMPIRE counter-drone systems.
sections.whyItMatters: Approval latency, not technology, has been the recurring bottleneck in fielding counter-drone systems. A 10-day review clock is a concrete, measurable change that could reshape how fast new interceptors and jammers reach units.

sections.heading: Kuwait Buys a $490M Nationwide Counter-Drone Shield From Britain's MARSS
sections.body:
Kuwait has agreed to purchase a 370-million-pound ($490.5 million) nationwide air-defense system from British firm MARSS, a subsidiary of Australia's Electro Optic Systems, to defend against unmanned aerial incursions. Per The Defense Post, MARSS will deploy a network of electro-optical, radar and sonar sensors linked to its NiDAR AI-driven command-and-control platform, combining soft-kill jammers with hard-kill interceptors, integrated over the coming 24 months.

UK Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard tied the deal to Task Force Sabre, London's framework for coordinating weapons and equipment distribution to Gulf partners — a program established in response to Iran's ongoing missile and drone barrages amid the wider US-Israel-Iran war. MARSS CEO Johannes Pinl said the project supports about 100 engineering and manufacturing roles at the company's Bristol plant.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a non-US, non-prime win in the Gulf counter-drone market, and it shows the UK using Task Force Sabre to convert Iran-war demand into British industrial output. Kuwait is buying an integrated command layer, not just interceptors — a sign buyers want the C2 architecture rather than piecemeal hardware.

sections.heading: Germany Approves Four More MEKO A-200 Frigates — Largest Surface Ship Order in TKMS History
sections.body:
Germany's Budget Committee approved the procurement of four additional MEKO A-200 DEU frigates from Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems (TKMS), lifting Berlin's total order to eight vessels after it scrapped the troubled F126 program with Dutch builder Damen, according to The Defense Post and the German defense ministry. TKMS CEO Oliver Burkhard called the eight-ship program the largest surface-vessel contract in the company's history.

The ships will focus on anti-submarine warfare for NATO operations in the Baltic and North Seas, the Atlantic and the High North. The first A-200 is scheduled for delivery in 2029. The vessel measures 121 meters, carries up to 125 sailors plus 40 troops, and can reach over 29 knots — sized to carry two light helicopters or unmanned aerial systems.
sections.whyItMatters: Germany is trading a delayed, over-complex program for a single-hulled, series-production class. Standardizing on one design simplifies training and sustainment and is aimed at closing a Baltic anti-submarine gap fast — a real test of whether European procurement reform can deliver on schedule.

sections.heading: Turkey's F-35 Return Still Blocked by CAATSA as Talks Intensify
sections.body:
Washington reaffirmed that the transfer of F-35s to Turkey remains conditional on Ankara resolving the S-400 issue, The Defense Post reported. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Greek outlet Kathimerini that President Trump wants to push the transfer of jets already paid for, but that 'until those conditions are met, the sale cannot go ahead.' CAATSA legislation bars the sale while Turkey retains the Russian S-400 system, a weapon incompatible with NATO networks.

Turkish Deputy Defense Minister Alpaslan Kavaklıoğlu struck an optimistic tone in Washington, telling CNN that 'intensive work' is underway on CAATSA and on returning the first six F-35s currently held in US storage — jets originally used for pilot training before Turkey was suspended from the program in 2019. The 2017 S-400 deal was worth approximately $2.5 billion.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between political intent in Washington and statutory prohibition is the whole story here. Turkey's reintegration would reshape NATO's eastern airpower and hand Lockheed a significant order — but it hinges on Ankara giving up or parking the S-400, which it has long refused.

sections.heading: India Sells Akash Missiles to Central Asia, Pushing Into Russia's Traditional Market
sections.body:
India has sold its Akash short-range air-defense missile system to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, confirmed by Indian Secretary for Defense Rajesh Kumar Singh, who did not disclose contract values, according to Bulgarian outlet fakti.bg citing money.bg and Defense News. The sales extend New Delhi's reach into a region historically dependent on Russian systems.

Indian military exports grew 62% to $4.1 billion in the last financial year, with missiles, armored vehicles, drones and ammunition supplied to over 80 countries. India's flagship export, the Russia-co-developed BrahMos supersonic cruise missile, has been contracted by the Philippines and Vietnam. Separately, Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said India is ready to co-develop and co-produce defense equipment — patrol vessels, radars and more — with ASEAN countries.
sections.whyItMatters: India is positioning itself as a politically neutral alternative supplier for states looking to reduce dependence on both Russian and Chinese systems. Winning Central Asian air-defense orders is symbolically significant: it cuts directly into Moscow's historic export turf.

bottomLine: The through-line today is acquisition speed. The US used AUSA to stand up new structures — AUTOWARCOM, Project Agincourt, Task Force Autonomous Warfare — and to open its drone marketplace to 33 nations while ordering counter-drone approvals compressed to days rather than months. Meanwhile Kuwait bought a British integrated counter-drone shield, Germany locked in eight TKMS frigates to fix a Baltic anti-submarine gap, and India sold Akash missiles into Central Asia. The common thread is that buyers and builders are reorganizing around drones, counter-drones and faster delivery — and the countries that can shorten the procurement cycle will win the next round of export orders. Watch whether Congress funds the $55 billion autonomy plan, since none of the US restructuring works without the money.
sources: Breaking Defense, Defense News, The Defense Post, UK Government (gov.uk), German Federal Ministry of Defence (bmvg.de), TKMS, Kathimerini, CNN Turk, fakti.bg (citing money.bg and Defense News), National Defense Magazine, Inside Unmanned Systems
